content.title: NASA's Orion capsule a key component to getting humans to the moon
content.text: BREVARD COUNTY, Fla. — Offering plenty of space for four crewmembers to work and live on board, the Orion spacecraft was designed to carry astronauts to the moon, and eventually deep space destinations. What You Need To Know Offering plenty of space for four crewmembers to work and live on board, the Orion spacecraft was designed to carry astronauts to the moon, and eventually deep space destinations The state-of-the-art vessel was built through a joint effort between Lockheed Martin and the European Space Agency It’s composed of the crew capsule, which can accommodate the astronauts for 21 days, and the European Service Module, which is the primary propulsion source The spacecraft provides life support, avionics, power, and the all-important thermal protection system that will ward off space radiation and the intense heat of re-entering Earth’s atmosphere Learn more about the Artemis mission The state-of-the-art vessel was built through a joint effort between Lockheed Martin and the European Space Agency. It’s composed of the crew capsule, which can accommodate the astronauts for 21 days, and the European Service Module, which is the primary propulsion source. “That little space craft right there is going to hold these four little humans, and we’re going to go on a nine-day journey, 250,000 miles away from Earth… that is pretty wicked awesome,” says Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman. The spacecraft provides life support, avionics, power, and the all-important thermal protection system that will ward off space radiation and the intense heat of re-entering Earth’s atmosphere. “They’ve called it the Apollo command module on steroids,” says Florida Tech Emeritus Faculty Bob Taylor. “It’s a lot bigger, it’s more comfortable, of course it has to hold four people.” That's compared to the Apollo 8 spacecraft, which held three astronauts. That December 1968 flight became the first crewed mission to leave Earth orbit and reach the moon. After 10 times around the moon, they returned home. “We’re a part of this mission that’s going back to the moon for the first time in over 50 years. It just adds this layer of wonderment and excitement,” says Artemis II Pilot Victor Glover. Now the Orion will take the Artemis astronauts on the same journey as its predecessor. And perhaps we will see another picture from the window of the Earthrise as before. “For a brief shining moment, it will bring Americans together, and maybe the world, just like Apollo 8 did,” Taylor says. One other key component of the Orion spacecraft is the launch abort system, which would bring astronauts to safety during a launch emergency.
